title: Tail-latency kernel handoff sweep (Nov 2027)
content:
Summary:

This doc captures a targeted sweep focused on tail-latency slices that appear correlated with cross-stream kernel handoffs during microbatch processing of text-generation workloads. The symptom chain: p99+ request latency spikes (~2-3x baseline) that align to small windows where SM occupancy drops then briefly saturates as a different kernel launches on the same SM set.

Why we ran this: customer reports of intermittent p99 bursts under 4–8 batch sizes, particularly on cold prefixes and when the KV cache misses occur. Prior occupancy runs showed no obvious low average occupancy; hypothesized cause is localized serialization at kernel boundaries (handoff) combined with async-copy and stream scheduling jitter.

Experiment setup:
- Model: LLaMA-variant (ca. 7B dense) served with quantized kernels (int8-ish) and standard KV-cache path.
- HW: 2x A100-SXM GPUs, PCIe disabled, nvlink enabled.
- Driver/CUDA/Nsight: NVIDIA driver 535.54, CUDA 12.2, Nsight Systems 2027.3.
- Runtime: rwinf-runtime@main (commit a7f9b2), custom scheduler flag enable_stream_preference=false.
- Capture mode: Nsight timeline + nvprof-style kernel-level timestamps (coarse) + custom NVTX spans added around batch handoff and KV cache apply.
- Workloads: three profiles
  - cold-single: single-request cold KV (prefix miss), batch_size=1
  - small-batched: burst of 8 requests with microbatch=2
  - warm-batched: repeated traffic with warmed KV cache

Key observations (timeline focused):
1) Repro pattern: in cold-single and small-batched runs p99 spikes map to a 200–700us window with: (a) trailing minimal activity across many SMs, (b) a short async-copy burst then (c) a sequence of small kernels launching on a subset of SMs.
2) Nsight timeline shows stream A kernel finishing, followed by stream B async-copy + small kernel on stream B; the hardware queues appear to prefer the copy+kernel pair leading to temporary eviction of longer-running persistent kernels from SM ownership (or effectively starving their next launch).
3) Measured per-kernel durations: larger matmul kernel ~900us, which normally overlaps with other ops. But when handoff occurs, we observe reduced concurrent occupancy for that kernel (SM fraction down 15–25%), increasing its wall time (itself blocking other work).
4) CUDA graph capture cases (captured graph with persistent-kernel style) largely avoid the handoff jitter — p99 improves ~30–45% — but graphs fail to cover dynamic KV cache apply steps which still trigger ad-hoc kernels and recreate the window.

Root-cause hypothesis (concise):
- Two effects amplify: (1) asymmetry in stream priority/ordering between async-copy streams and compute streams, and (2) serialization caused by small kernel launches that flush scheduling quanta on a subset of SMs. The combination makes the long matmul kernel lose effective concurrency momentarily, increasing tail latency.

Micro-analyses and metrics extracted:
- SM occupancy heatmap (frame-level): windows with handoff show 0.55 average occupancy dropping to 0.38 on the matmul hot-path SMs.
- Kernel launch latency distribution: small-kernel-launch jitter increases p95 of launch latency by ~120us during handoff windows.
- NVTX correlation: NVTX span "kv_apply" precedes the jitter windows consistently.

Mitigation experiments and results:
1) Stream priority bump (assign async-copy streams lower priority than compute): reduced p99 spikes by ~20% on small-batched, but added modest overhead to throughput when KV miss rate was high.
2) Preflight batching of KV-applies: collect KV ops into a single larger kernel where possible — reduces number of small kernels launched per request; p99 improved 35% in cold-single. Tradeoff: more memory pressure and code complexity.
3) Persistent-kernel / kernel-fusion attempts: fused small kernels into the persistent kernel to eliminate handoff entirely. This gave the best p99 reduction (~50%) but required invasive runtime changes and some performance regression in the steady-state due to larger register pressure.
4) CUDA graph with dynamic node fallback: captured most of the steady path into a graph and left a minimal dynamic node for KV apply. This lowered baseline tail but produced occasional fallback-path spikes; overall p99 improved 30% while p50 unchanged.

Notable microbench numbers (representative):
- Baseline small-batched p99: 1.8s
- Stream-priority mitigation p99: 1.46s
- KV batching p99: 1.2s
- Persistent-fusion p99: 0.9s (but p50 +6% overhead)
- CUDA-graph hybrid p99: 1.26s

Operational notes from captures:
- nsight symbology: red vertical markers are NVTX flush points; look for immediate following white-block small kernels.
- Observed driver preemption events roughly coincident with handoff windows on one run; suggests scheduling thrash between compute queues.
- No evidence of PCIe stalls; async copies were NVL-linked and fast.

Short-term recommendations (high priority):
- Enable stream priority knob with a conservative lower priority for memory-copy streams in cloud images; rollout as an opt-in toggle for affected customers. (Owner: Diego)
- Add a short-term SDK opt that coalesces KV apply ops into batched kernels when microbatch<=4. (Owner: Liam)

Medium-term / engineering work:
- Prototype persistent-kernel fusion for KV apply path (risk: register pressure). If fusion not feasible, explore selective inline fusion for the tails of matmul to reduce cross-kernel boundaries. (Owner: eng-serving-runtime core team)
- Improve CUDA graph coverage: investigate graph-with-ephemeral-node patterns where dynamic KV nodes are scheduled with minimal launch overhead. (Spike owner: Priya)
- Add deterministic test in perf harness to reproduce handoff window using synthetic KV miss ratio and microbatch sizes; include an Nsight trace artifact to make triage reproducible.

Open questions / TODOs:
- How do newer drivers (post-535) change scheduler behavior? Need a quick matrix test across 535, 540, 545 drivers.
- Can we instrument kernel owners at SM granularity to detect which kernels are evicted/blocked during the window? (requires deeper hw counters)
- Explore whether stream aggregation (single stream for compute+copy but with dependency graph) reduces launch jitter without impacting throughput.

Appendix (quick checklists):
- Reproduce steps (short):
  1) Start runtime with enable_stream_preference=false and nsight capture enabled
  2) Run cold-single profile (single request with KV miss) x100
  3) Collect timeline, export NVTX spans, and grep for "kv_apply" followed by small kernels
- Useful commands:
  - nsys profile --trace=cuda,nvtx --output=hand-off.nsys ./run_profile.sh
  - python tools/parse_nsight.py hand-off.nsys --span kv_apply --window 1000

Action items (owners):
- Diego: add stream-priority flag and run cluster-wide smoke test by 2027-11-24
- Liam: push KV batching opt into feature-branch and benchmark steady-state throughput impact by 2027-11-28
- Priya: spike CUDA-graph hybrid pattern and report findings by 2027-12-05

Notes-to-self / freeform:
- This feels like a class of problem that shows up when you have many small ephemeral kernels interacting with a small set of persistent heavy kernels. Worth drafting a short playbook for kernel-handoff debugging with standard Nsight markers and a small artifact set (trace + filtered kernel list + SM-occupancy heatmap).
- Save example trace for post-mortem library under /perf/artifacts/hand-off-nov-2027 (uploaded)

End of doc.
